title: The Industrial Revolution Picks Up Steam
summary: Steam engines pumped water out of coal mines, coal melted iron, and iron built even more engines, in a giant loop that kept growing. Soon steam was hammering, printing newspapers and showing off in a huge glass palace in London. Then the new way of making things spread to Belgium, France, Germany, America and Japan.

sections.heading: A Revolution in Slow Motion
paragraphs: When you hear the word 'revolution', you might picture something sudden: crowds in the street, a king losing his crown, everything changing in a week. The Industrial Revolution was not like that at all. It was more like a tide coming in. If you stood on the beach and watched for five minutes, you would hardly notice the water moving. Come back after a few hours, and the whole beach has disappeared.

Historians use the name 'Industrial Revolution' for the huge change in how people made things, which began in Britain in roughly the 1760s and is often said to have run until about the 1830s or 1840s, before spreading to other countries. During those years, more and more work moved from hands, homes and small workshops to machines, factories and mines. Instead of most people growing food on farms, more and more people made goods, dug coal, smelted iron and worked in towns. The name became popular in English in the 1880s, when the historian Arnold Toynbee gave lectures about it at Oxford, but French writers had used similar words decades earlier.

Not every historian likes the word 'revolution'. Some, such as John Clapham in the early 1900s and Nicholas Crafts more recently, pointed out that Britain's economy grew fairly slowly in those decades, maybe one or two percent a year, not in a sudden leap. In 1830, most British workers still did not work in factories. Lots of cloth was still woven on hand looms, many mills still turned with waterwheels (as we saw in the last part), and farm work still employed huge numbers of people. So the change was real and enormous, but it built up step by step over a lifetime and more.

Imagine a grandmother born in a Lancashire village in 1760. As a girl she might have spun wool by the fire and walked everywhere. By the time she was an old woman in the 1830s, her grandchildren might be working in a mill with a steam engine thumping in the basement, buying cheap printed cotton dresses, and reading newspapers printed by steam. She would have seen her world transformed, even though no single year felt like an earthquake.

Why did it start in Britain? Historians still argue about this, and there is no single answer. Britain had lots of coal close to the surface and close to the sea or rivers, so it could be moved cheaply. Wages for workers were fairly high compared with the price of coal, which made it worth paying for machines that saved labour. The country had a big trading network, banks, canals that were being dug in the 1760s and 1770s, a large market at home and overseas, and a culture of tinkerers, instrument makers and engineers who shared ideas in clubs and societies, like the Lunar Society of Birmingham that Matthew Boulton belonged to. Part of Britain's trade and wealth also came from its empire and from the enslaved labour that grew cotton and sugar, a hard truth we will look at honestly in Part 15.

Steam was not the only cause of the Industrial Revolution. In fact, the first great spinning mills ran on water. But steam became its beating heart, because it could provide power anywhere, at any time, in any amount you could afford coal for. And steam connected everything else together, as we are about to see in one of the most important loops in history.

sections.heading: Coal, Iron and Steam: The Great Loop
paragraphs: Think of three friends who each make the others stronger. That is how coal, iron and steam worked together.

Step one: steam engines pumped water out of coal mines, so miners could dig deeper and bring up more coal. Step two: coal (turned into a fuel called coke) was used to melt iron out of iron ore in furnaces, so iron became cheaper and more plentiful. Step three: that cheaper iron was used to build more steam engines, plus pumps, rails, bridges and machines. And more steam engines meant more pumped mines, more coal, more iron, and round and round the loop went, getting bigger every turn.

The loop needed one big discovery first. For thousands of years, iron had been smelted using charcoal, which is made by slowly burning wood. But making charcoal needed huge amounts of wood, and as we saw in Part 1, Britain's forests were shrinking. In 1709, at Coalbrookdale in Shropshire, an ironmaster named Abraham Darby began fuelling his blast furnace with coke instead. Coke is made by baking coal to drive off its tar and gases, leaving a hard, almost pure carbon fuel. Coke was cheaper, mainly because it took far less labour than cutting trees and burning charcoal, and Britain had plenty of coal.

A blast furnace is a tall tower filled with layers of iron ore, fuel and limestone. To get hot enough to melt iron, it needs a powerful, steady blast of air blown in at the bottom, just as blowing on a campfire makes it blaze. For centuries, that blast came from big leather bellows worked by waterwheels. That meant ironworks had to sit beside rivers, and in a dry summer the furnace might have to stop.

Steam changed that, at first in a roundabout way. At Coalbrookdale in 1742, a steam engine was used to pump water back up into a reservoir above the works, so that the waterwheel could keep turning even when the stream was low. Later, engineers connected steam engines directly to huge blowing cylinders, which were giant air pumps. One of the first Boulton & Watt engines, in 1776, blew air for John Wilkinson's furnace at New Willey in Shropshire. Now an ironworks could be built wherever there was coal and ore, and it could run all year round.

More inventions kept the loop spinning faster. In 1784, Henry Cort patented 'puddling', a way of stirring melted iron in a special furnace to make strong wrought iron using coal instead of charcoal. In 1828, James Beaumont Neilson in Scotland patented the 'hot blast', which heated the air before it was blown into the furnace and cut the fuel needed by about a third.

The results were astonishing. In 1720, British furnaces using charcoal made about 20,000 tons of iron a year. By 1806, furnaces using coke were producing around 250,000 tons. By the 1790s Britain, which once had to import much of its iron from places like Sweden and Russia, had become an exporter of iron instead. Iron began appearing everywhere: in the world's first big cast-iron bridge, the Iron Bridge over the River Severn near Coalbrookdale, put up in 1779 and opened to traffic in 1781; in pipes, rails, pots, machine frames, columns and, of course, steam-engine cylinders. Later in the 1800s, new methods such as Henry Bessemer's converter (1856) made cheap steel, an even stronger metal, and the loop grew bigger again.

sections.heading: Black Diamonds: Counting the Coal
paragraphs: If the Industrial Revolution had a fuel gauge, it would be the amount of coal Britain dug out of the ground. People sometimes called coal 'black diamonds', because so much wealth came from it. The numbers tell an amazing story.

Around 1700, Britain mined just under 3 million tons of coal a year. By the 1770s, the figure had climbed to roughly 6 million tons. By 1815 it was about 16 million tons, and by 1830 more than 30 million. Then it really took off. By about 1900, British mines were producing over 200 million tonnes a year, and output reached its all-time peak in 1913, at about 287 million tonnes. That is roughly a hundred times more than in 1700.

Where did all this coal go? Some went into homes for cooking and heating, as it had for centuries. But more and more fed the new industrial world: ironworks and their blast furnaces; factories, mills and workshops with steam engines; gasworks that baked coal to make gas for street lights; brickworks, potteries, glassworks and breweries; steamships and, of course, railway locomotives. Britain also sold huge amounts of coal abroad, shipping it to ports all over the world.

Steam was needed to get the coal out, too. As mines went deeper, steam engines did more than pump water. They wound cages and tubs up and down the shafts, and later they drove big fans that sucked stale air and dangerous gases out of the tunnels. Before steam-powered fans, miners often kept a fire burning at the bottom of one shaft so that the rising hot air would pull fresh air through the mine. In Belgium, steam pumps helped some mines go from about 220 metres deep in 1790 to an average of about 440 metres by 1866, with one pit more than 1,000 metres deep.

More coal meant more miners. Around 1841, Britain had about 216,000 coal miners. By 1920, the industry employed more than 1.1 million people. Mining was hard and dangerous work, and for many years it included children. We will look carefully at that side of the story in Part 15.

Coal gave Britain a special advantage. A single tonne of coal holds more energy than a strong horse could deliver in a couple of years of hard daily work, even though early engines wasted most of it as heat. By digging up the remains of ancient forests that had been squashed underground for hundreds of millions of years, Britain was in a sense borrowing energy from the deep past, and steam engines were the machines that turned that stored sunshine into motion.

sections.heading: Machines That Make Machines
paragraphs: Here is a puzzle. To build a good steam engine, you need parts that fit together very accurately: a perfectly round cylinder, a piston that slides snugly inside it, screws and bolts that fit their nuts. But in the 1700s, almost every part was shaped by hand with files, chisels and hammers. Two screws made by the same craftsman might not even fit the same nut. How do you get accurate parts? You build accurate machines that make them. Engineers call these 'machine tools': machines whose job is to cut, drill, plane and shape metal to make other machines.

The star of this story is Henry Maudslay, born in 1771 in Woolwich, near London. As a boy he worked filling cartridges at the Royal Arsenal and then in its blacksmith's shop, where he became famous for his skill with metal. As a young man he worked for the inventor Joseph Bramah, and he helped build Bramah's famous 'unpickable' lock. Bramah put one in his shop window with a sign offering a reward to anyone who could pick it. It stayed unpicked for 47 years, and Maudslay also designed special tools so the locks could be made in large numbers at a sensible price.

Around 1800, in his own workshop in London, Maudslay built one of the first practical screw-cutting lathes. A lathe spins a piece of metal while a sharp cutting tool shaves it into shape. Maudslay's lathe held the cutting tool firmly in a sliding rest, moved along by an accurate master screw and a set of change gears, so it could cut screw threads that were exactly the same every time. He did not invent each of these pieces, but he combined them brilliantly. Suddenly, nuts and bolts could be standardised: any nut of a given size would fit any bolt of that size.

Maudslay also worked with the engineer Marc Isambard Brunel (father of the famous Isambard Kingdom Brunel) to build 42 machines for the Royal Navy's block mills at Portsmouth, finished in the 1800s. They made pulley blocks for sailing ships, which needed huge numbers of them. With the machines, about ten unskilled workers could do the work that had needed about 110 skilled craftsmen. It was one of the earliest examples of a factory where a series of special machines did each step of a job. Maudslay also built a measuring machine, a bench micrometer, accurate to about one ten-thousandth of an inch. His workers nicknamed it 'the Lord Chancellor', because, like a top judge, it settled any argument about whether a piece of work was accurate.

Maudslay's workshop became a kind of engineering school. Among those who trained there were Joseph Whitworth, who in 1841 proposed a standard system of screw threads that was adopted across Britain; Richard Roberts, who built improved machine tools and a self-acting spinning mule; and a young Scot named James Nasmyth.

Nasmyth, born in Edinburgh in 1808, was the son of a painter and had been building model steam engines since boyhood. He set up his own works, the Bridgewater Foundry at Patricroft near Manchester. In 1839 a problem landed on his desk: the engineers building the giant ship Great Britain wanted an iron paddle-wheel shaft about 30 inches (76 centimetres) thick. No hammer in Britain was big enough to forge it. On 24 November 1839, Nasmyth sketched an answer in his notebook: a heavy iron block, the ram, lifted straight up by a steam cylinder above it, then dropped onto the hot metal. The ship ended up with a propeller instead of paddle wheels, so that shaft was never needed, but the idea was too good to waste.

Here the story has a twist about fair credit. In France, an engineer named François Bourdon at the Schneider works at Le Creusot had a similar idea, and he built the first working steam hammer in 1840. When Nasmyth visited Le Creusot in April 1842, Bourdon is said to have taken him to the forge to 'see his own child'. Nasmyth patented his own design on 9 December 1842. He built his first hammer at his own Patricroft works, and in 1843 the Low Moor ironworks in Bradford took an improved version. His works manager, Robert Wilson, later added a clever self-acting valve gear that let the operator choose exactly how hard each blow would be. Nasmyth was a brilliant self-promoter, so for a long time he got most of the credit, but historians now recognise both men.

The steam hammer was astonishingly controllable. Nasmyth loved to show it off by placing an egg in a wineglass and bringing the ram down so gently that it cracked the egg without breaking the glass. Then, with the next blow, he could make the whole building shake. Steam hammers grew to giant sizes: the Krupp works in Germany built one in 1861 nicknamed 'Fritz', known as a 50-ton hammer. They forged ship shafts, anchors, locomotive parts and armour plate. Machines were now making the heavy parts for other machines, and the steam engine was helping to build its own children.

sections.heading: Printing by Steam
paragraphs: Picture a London printing shop in 1800. Two men work a wooden hand press. One dabs sticky ink onto the metal type with leather balls on handles. The other lays a sheet of paper on top, slides the bed under a heavy flat plate, and heaves on a long bar to press the paper down. Lift, peel, hang the sheet to dry, repeat. A good team might manage only a few hundred sheets an hour. The press itself was not so different from the one Johannes Gutenberg had used in Mainz about 350 years earlier. For a busy newspaper that needed thousands of copies by morning, that was a real problem.

The answer came from a German printer named Friedrich Koenig, born in Eisleben in 1774. He moved to London in 1806, because Britain had the money and engineering skill he needed, and he worked with a German watchmaker and engineer named Andreas Friedrich Bauer. Koenig received a patent in 1810, and his first trial machine ran in April 1812.

Koenig's big idea was to stop pressing the paper flat. Instead, the sheet was wrapped around a rotating cylinder, which rolled over the inked type as the type bed slid back and forth beneath it. Rollers, rather than leather balls, spread the ink, and a steam engine drove the whole thing, so the workers only had to feed in blank sheets and take away printed ones.

One of Koenig's visitors was John Walter, the owner of The Times newspaper. He ordered two of the new machines. According to the story told by The Times itself, they were set up quietly in a building next door, partly because Walter feared the hand pressmen might protest or damage machines that threatened their jobs. On the morning of 29 November 1814, readers of The Times opened their paper to discover that it told them something remarkable: the very sheet they were holding had been printed by steam-driven machinery. The machines could print about 1,100 sheets an hour, several times faster than a hand press.

Koenig's later machines printed both sides of the paper in one pass. In 1817, after a disagreement with his London business partner, the printer Thomas Bensley, Koenig went home to Germany. He and Bauer set up a factory in an old abandoned monastery at Oberzell near Würzburg. Their company, Koenig & Bauer, still makes printing presses today, more than 200 years later.

The results reached almost every home. As taxes on newspapers were cut (the British stamp duty on newspapers was lowered in 1836 and abolished in 1855), cheap 'penny' papers appeared, and millions of ordinary people could read the news every day. Steam presses also printed cheap books, magazines, school readers, posters, railway timetables and maps. Steam helped spread not just goods, but ideas.

sections.heading: A Palace of Glass: The Great Exhibition of 1851
paragraphs: On 1 May 1851, Queen Victoria opened the most extraordinary building London had ever seen. In Hyde Park stood a giant greenhouse of iron and glass, about 563 metres (1,848 feet) long and 138 metres (454 feet) wide, so tall in the middle that full-grown elm trees fitted inside it. A magazine called it the 'Crystal Palace', and the name stuck.

The building was designed by Joseph Paxton, who had started as a gardener and had built huge glass greenhouses for the Duke of Devonshire at Chatsworth. His design was a clever kit. Thousands of identical iron columns, girders and wooden glazing bars, plus hundreds of thousands of panes of glass made mostly in Birmingham and Smethwick, were mass-produced and bolted together on site. From planning to opening took only about nine months. The Crystal Palace was itself a product of the Industrial Revolution: cheap iron, factory-made glass and parts that fitted together because machine tools had made them accurately.

Its official name was the Great Exhibition of the Works of Industry of All Nations. The idea was pushed forward by Prince Albert, Queen Victoria's husband, and the civil servant Henry Cole. It was the first in a long series of world's fairs. Inside were about 13,000 exhibits from Britain, its colonies and 44 foreign countries.

Imagine walking down the long central hall. You might see huge raw lumps of coal and iron ore, then gleaming locomotives and marine engines, printing presses, looms and spinning machines. In the machinery section, many machines were shown actually working, driven by steam piped in from boilers outside the building, so visitors could watch cotton being spun and cloth woven in front of their eyes. From the United States came a mechanical reaping machine for harvesting grain and Samuel Colt's revolvers. From France came fine silks and porcelain.

Between May and October 1851, about six million visits were recorded, at a time when Great Britain had roughly 21 million people. On the busiest day, 7 October, nearly 110,000 people crowded in. Tickets were expensive at first, but from late May there were cheaper 'shilling days', and special trains brought workers and their families from industrial towns all over the country. For many, it was their first trip to London.

The exhibition made a profit of about £186,000. That money helped buy land in South Kensington, where museums grew up, including the Victoria and Albert Museum, the Natural History Museum and the Science Museum, which today displays some of the most important steam engines in the world. The Crystal Palace itself was taken down and rebuilt, even larger, at Sydenham in south London, where it stood until it burned down in 1936.

The Great Exhibition showed Britain at the height of its industrial lead. People began calling Britain 'the workshop of the world'. Around the middle of the 1800s, Britain produced a very large share of the world's manufactured goods: by some historians' estimates about a fifth of everything, and far more of the world's iron, coal and cotton cloth. But visitors who looked closely at the American and European exhibits could already see that other countries were catching up fast.

sections.heading: Steam Goes Around the World
paragraphs: Britain tried to keep its industrial secrets at home. For many years it was against the law for skilled workers to emigrate and for some kinds of machinery to be exported. But ideas, like steam, are hard to keep bottled up. Engineers moved abroad, machines were copied, and soon other countries were building their own industries, often with their own brilliant inventors.

Belgium was the first country on the European continent to industrialise on a big scale, helped by rich coalfields and iron ore. An English machine-builder, William Cockerill, moved there in 1799 and built spinning machinery for the wool town of Verviers. His son John Cockerill, born in Lancashire in 1790, set up a huge works at Seraing near Liège in 1817, in a former palace of the Prince-Bishops of Liège. It combined an iron foundry, blast furnaces and a machine factory, and by 1840 it had sixteen steam engines and about 3,000 workers. It built steam engines, ships' engines and, in 1835, Belgium's first steam locomotive.

France followed, with its own engineering tradition. In 1836, the brothers Adolphe and Eugène Schneider took over the ironworks at Le Creusot in Burgundy, which grew into one of Europe's greatest engineering works, building locomotives, ships, bridges and steam engines. That is where François Bourdon built his steam hammer in 1840.

In Germany, the great coal deposits of the Ruhr valley became the engine room of the country. Ruhr coal output grew from about 2 million tons in 1850 to about 60 million by 1900 and more than 110 million by 1913. Companies like Krupp of Essen, famous for its steel and its giant 'Fritz' hammer, grew into industrial empires. After Germany became one united country in 1871, its industry raced ahead, and by around 1900 it was making more steel than Britain.

The United States had vast forests, rivers and coalfields, and plenty of inventors of its own, such as Oliver Evans and George Corliss, whom we have already met. American coal output shot up from about 8 million tons in 1850 to about 270 million tons in 1900. By around 1900, the United States had become the largest industrial economy in the world.

Perhaps the most dramatic change happened in Japan. For more than two centuries, Japan had strictly limited contact with the outside world. In 1853, American steam-powered warships arrived in Tokyo Bay, and the Japanese were shocked to see ships moving against the wind with smoke pouring from their funnels. In 1868, a new government took power in the name of the young Emperor Meiji, and set out to learn from the industrial countries as fast as possible.

Japanese leaders travelled to the United States and Europe on the Iwakura Mission (1871 to 1873) to study factories, schools and governments. Japan hired foreign experts, but always with the aim of training Japanese engineers to take over. In 1872 the government opened the Tomioka Silk Mill in Gunma Prefecture, designed with the help of the French engineer Paul Brunat. A single-cylinder steam engine powered its silk-reeling machines, and it started with about 210 young women workers, many of them daughters of former samurai families. The mill ran until 1987 and is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

By 1900, steam was at work on every inhabited continent, in mines, mills, workshops and printing houses. But so far we have mostly seen steam staying in one place, turning machines. The most exciting question was still waiting: could steam carry people and goods across water and along roads, faster and farther than any horse or sail?

deepDive: Why did the Industrial Revolution start in Britain, and how important was steam? Historians are still arguing, and the debate is a great example of how history works. The economic historian Robert Allen has argued that Britain had an unusual combination of high wages and very cheap coal. When workers are expensive and energy is cheap, it pays to invent machines that replace muscle with coal-fired power, which is exactly what steam engines did. Joel Mokyr stresses something different: an 'Industrial Enlightenment', a culture in which scientists, instrument makers and craftsmen shared knowledge through societies, books and letters. Kenneth Pomeranz, comparing Britain with the richest parts of China, argued that two strokes of luck mattered a great deal: coal deposits located near where they were needed, and overseas colonies and trade that supplied land-hungry products like cotton, sugar and timber, much of it produced by enslaved people. Most historians now think several of these factors worked together. There is also a surprise about timing. When economists measure growth, steam seems to have contributed only a little to Britain's productivity before about 1830, because engines were still expensive, wasteful of coal and few in number compared with waterwheels, horses and hand tools. In a 2004 study, Nicholas Crafts estimated that steam's biggest economic impact came after about 1850, when high-pressure engines, cheap iron, steamships and railways spread widely. This fits a pattern seen with other 'general purpose technologies' such as electricity and computers: their full effects can take many decades to arrive, because people must invent new ways of organising work around them. Numbers also need care. Early coal and iron figures were collected inconsistently and are estimates, and 'tons' in older British records usually means long tons of 2,240 pounds, slightly more than a metric tonne. Even so, the overall picture is clear: between 1700 and 1913 British coal output grew roughly a hundredfold, and that river of fuel, turned into motion by steam engines, reshaped the world economy.
funFact: James Nasmyth liked to show how delicately his giant steam hammer could be controlled by using it to crack an egg standing in a wineglass without breaking the glass.
